Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a “recipe” for how you would use the two tools you described to place a McDonald’s order for a burger and fries. I’ll walk through the whole flow, from discovery to execution, and point out the practical details you’ll need to handle along the way. --- ## 1. Discover the right API | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Search** | Use the *search‑internet* tool to look for “McDonald’s ordering API”, “McDonald’s mobile app API”, “McDonald’s digital ordering endpoint”, or “McDonald’s delivery API”. | McDonald’s doesn’t publish a public API, so you’ll either find an internal endpoint (unlikely) or a third‑party service that talks to McDonald’s (e.g., DoorDash, UberEats, Grubhub). | | **Inspect results** | Open the top 3–5 links, skim the documentation or code snippets, and note:
• Base URL
• Authentication method (OAuth, API key, cookie, etc.)
• Required headers
• Request payload structure
• Response format | You need this information to build a valid request later. | > **Tip:** If you can’t find a public McDonald’s endpoint, the most reliable path is to use a delivery platform’s API that already has a McDonald’s partner integration. --- ## 2. Gather required data | Data | Where it comes from | Notes | |------|---------------------|-------| | **Location** | User’s address or GPS coordinates | Needed to find the nearest McDonald’s and to calculate delivery time. | | **Payment method** | Credit‑card token, PayPal ID, or stored payment profile | Most APIs require a token rather than raw card numbers. | | **Menu items** | Item IDs for “burger” and “fries” | These IDs come from the menu catalog endpoint of the chosen API. | | **Order modifiers** | Size, toppings, special instructions | Optional but often required for a complete order. | | **User identifiers** | Session ID, user ID, or device token | Needed for authentication or to attach the order to a user account. | > **Practical note:** If you’re using a third‑party service, you’ll usually get a “menu catalog” endpoint that lists all items with their IDs. You can hard‑code the IDs for a standard burger and fries or fetch them dynamically. --- ## 3. Authenticate | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Obtain credentials** | Register an app or obtain an API key from the chosen platform. | Most APIs require an API key or OAuth token. | | **Login / token exchange** | If OAuth is used, perform the authorization code flow or client‑credentials flow to get an access token. | The token will be sent in the `Authorization` header (`Bearer `). | | **Store token** | Keep the token in memory for the duration of the request. | Tokens usually expire after a short period. | > **Example header**: > `Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...` --- ## 4. Build the order payload A typical payload looks like this (JSON): ```json { "location": { "latitude": 37.7749, "longitude": -122.4194 }, "payment_method_id": "pm_1234567890", "items": [ { "product_id": "burger_001", "quantity": 1, "options": { "size": "medium", "toppings": ["lettuce", "tomato"] } }, { "product_id": "fries_001", "quantity": 1, "options": { "size": "large" } } ], "special_instructions": "Please ring the bell when ready." } ``` > **Key points** > * `product_id` must match the catalog ID. > * `quantity` is an integer. > * `options` is optional but often required for size or toppings. > * The `location` field can be a lat/lon pair or a formatted address, depending on the API. --- ## 5. Execute the API call | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Choose the endpoint** | From the discovery step, pick the “create order” or “place order” URL. | This is the endpoint that will create the order. | | **Set headers** | `Content-Type: application/json`, `Accept: application/json`, `Authorization: Bearer `. | These are the minimal headers most APIs expect. | | **Send the request** | Use the *execute‑API-call* tool, passing the URL, headers, and JSON body. | The tool will perform the HTTP POST and return the response. | | **Handle the response** | Parse the JSON. Look for fields like `order_id`, `status`, `estimated_delivery_time`. | These confirm that the order was accepted. | > **Example call** (pseudo‑code for the tool): ```json { "url": "https://api.doordash.com/v1/orders", "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json", "Authorization": "Bearer " }, "params": {}, "body": { /* the JSON payload above */ } } ``` --- ## 6. Verify and follow up | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Check status** | If the API returns a status of “queued” or “processing”, poll the “order status” endpoint until it becomes “confirmed” or “delivered”. | Some services require polling to get the final state. | | **Handle errors** | If the response contains an error code (e.g., 400, 401, 403, 500), interpret it and retry or abort. | Robust error handling prevents silent failures. | | **Notify the user** | Send a confirmation message (e.g., “Your burger and fries are on the way! Order #12345, ETA 25 min”). | Keeps the user informed. | --- ## 7. Clean up | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Refresh token** | If the access token is close to expiry, refresh it for future orders. | Keeps the session alive. | | **Log the transaction** | Store the order ID, timestamp, and any relevant metadata for audit or support. | Useful for troubleshooting or refunds. | --- ## Summary Flow Diagram ``` [Search API] → [Inspect Docs] → [Collect Data] → [Authenticate] ↓ ↓ [Build Payload] → [Execute Call] → [Parse Response] ↓ ↓ [Poll Status] → [Handle Errors] → [Notify User] ↓ [Cleanup & Log] ``` --- ### What if McDonald’s has no public API? If your search turns up nothing, the most pragmatic route is: 1. **Pick a delivery partner** (DoorDash, UberEats, Grubhub, etc.) that lists McDonald’s as a restaurant. 2. **Use that partner’s API** – they already have the necessary integration. 3. **Follow the same steps** above, substituting the partner’s endpoints and authentication scheme. --- ### Final Checklist - [ ] Search for McDonald’s or partner APIs. - [ ] Identify authentication method. - [ ] Gather location, payment, and menu item IDs. - [ ] Build JSON payload. - [ ] Execute POST request. - [ ] Poll for status if needed. - [ ] Handle errors and confirm to user. With these steps, you can programmatically place a burger and fries order from McDonald’s (or a partner) using the two tools you have. Happy coding—and enjoy your meal!
